title: CIA4U Exit Card Learning Package
problemAnchor: 本节课的核心概念（Aggregate Demand Components、Downward-Sloping AD Curve、AD Curve Shifters、Long-Run Aggregate Supply）之间有什么联系？学生在理解上最容易卡在哪里？

abt.and: 你已经完成了本节课的学习。
abt.but: 但是这 7 个知识节点之间可能存在 7 种典型错误理解，学生容易记住零散规则却在综合判断时互相打架。
abt.therefore: 系统先诊断你卡在哪个知识节点，再用对应补救模块带你重新理解，最后用复测确认是否真正连起来。

objective: Aggregate demand (AD) is the total spending in the economy, composed of household consumption (C), business investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports (X - M), matching the GDP expenditure approach.；The AD curve slopes downward due to three effects: the wealth effect (higher price levels reduce real wealth and consumption), the interest rate effect (higher prices increase demand for money, raising interest rates and reducing investment), and the foreign trade effect (higher domestic prices reduce net exports).；The AD curve shifts when there are changes in government expenditure, money supply, or tax rates (factors beyond the price level).

learningGoals.statement: Identify and explain the components of aggregate demand and the reasons for the downward-sloping AD curve.
Distinguish between movements along the AD curve and shifts of the AD curve.
Explain the difference between short-run and long-run aggregate supply and the transition to long-run equilibrium.
Analyze the effects of supply shocks on output, employment, and the price level.

knowledgeNodes.name: Aggregate Demand Components
knowledgeNodes.definition: Aggregate demand (AD) is the total planned spending on final goods and services in an economy at a given price level. It consists of four components: household consumption (C), business investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports (X - M). This composition mirrors the expenditure approach to GDP.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.

knowledgeNodes.name: Downward-Sloping AD Curve
knowledgeNodes.definition: The aggregate demand curve slopes downward because of three effects: (1) Wealth effect – a lower price level increases the real value of money and wealth, boosting consumption. (2) Interest rate effect – lower prices reduce money demand, lowering interest rates and stimulating investment. (3) Foreign trade effect – lower domestic prices make exports cheaper and imports more expensive, raising net exports.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.

knowledgeNodes.name: AD Curve Shifters
knowledgeNodes.definition: The entire AD curve shifts left or right when there are changes in autonomous spending factors that are not caused by a change in the price level. Key shifters include changes in government expenditure, money supply, and tax rates.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of fiscal policy in Canada, including how it is shaped and its impact.

knowledgeNodes.name: Long-Run Aggregate Supply
knowledgeNodes.definition: The long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve is vertical at the economy’s potential output (full-employment real GDP). In the long run, output depends only on supply-side factors—capital, labour, and technology—and is independent of the price level.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.

knowledgeNodes.name: Short-Run Aggregate Supply
knowledgeNodes.definition: The short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve is relatively flat, reflecting sticky wages and prices. In the short run, output is determined primarily by aggregate demand and can differ from potential output; firms adjust production rather than prices.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.

knowledgeNodes.name: Supply Shocks
knowledgeNodes.definition: A supply shock is an unexpected event that shifts the SRAS curve. Adverse supply shocks (e.g., sudden oil price increase) reduce output, raise unemployment, and raise the price level (stagflation). Favourable supply shocks (e.g., technological breakthroughs) increase output and may lower prices.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.

knowledgeNodes.name: Short-Run to Long-Run Adjustment
knowledgeNodes.nameEn: Transition from Short-Run to Long-Run Equilibrium
knowledgeNodes.definition: When the economy operates above full-employment output, tight labour and resource markets bid up wages and input prices. Higher production costs shift the SRAS curve upward until real GDP returns to its potential level, restoring long-run equilibrium.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.

Distinguish between movements along the AD curve and shifts of the AD curve.
Explain the difference between short-run and long-run aggregate supply and the transition to long-run equilibrium.

questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies all four components of aggregate demand (C+I+G+NX).
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.
questions.alignmentNote: AD components are part of macroeconomic models in D1.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student knows AD includes investment, government, and net exports beyond consumption.
questions.commonMisconception: Aggregate demand only refers to household consumption spending.
questions.stem: Aggregate demand (AD) is composed of which of the following sets of spending components?

options.label: A
options.text: Household consumption (C), business investment (I), government spending (G), net exports (X - M)
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! AD equals C + I + G + (X - M), matching the expenditure approach to GDP.

options.label: B
options.text: Business investment (I) and government spending (G) only
options.feedbackWrong: This omits consumption and net exports. AD includes all spending on final goods and services.

options.label: C
options.text: Household consumption (C) and government spending (G) only
options.feedbackWrong: Investment and net exports are also part of AD. Think of the expenditure formula for GDP.

options.label: D
options.feedbackWrong: Consumption is the largest component, but AD includes business investment, government spending, and net exports as well.

options.label: E
options.text: Business investment (I) and net exports (X - M) only
options.feedbackWrong: Consumption and government spending are also part of AD. AD is the total of all spending sectors.

questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies the wealth effect as operating through real wealth changes due to price level changes.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.
questions.alignmentNote: Wealth effect is part of the downward-sloping AD curve in macroeconomic models.
questions.stemIntent: Check understanding of the wealth effect mechanism.
questions.commonMisconception: The wealth effect refers only to financial asset values or stock market wealth.
questions.stem: According to the wealth effect, a decrease in the overall price level will:

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the real value of money and financial assets, leading to more consumption
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! A lower price level increases real wealth, encouraging households to spend more.

options.label: B
options.text: Decrease the purchasing power of money, reducing consumption
options.feedbackWrong: A decrease in the price level actually increases purchasing power. The wealth effect works in the opposite direction.

options.label: C
options.text: Only affect stock market wealth but not real spending
options.feedbackWrong: The wealth effect applies to the real value of all nominal assets, not just stocks. It affects overall consumption.

options.label: D
options.text: Have no effect on consumption because wages are sticky
options.feedbackWrong: Sticky wages affect supply, not the wealth effect. The wealth effect operates through real balances and assets.

questions.successCriteria: Student distinguishes a shift of AD from a movement along AD caused by price level change.
questions.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of fiscal policy in Canada, including how it is shaped and its impact.
questions.alignmentNote: AD shifters like government spending are fiscal policy tools from D2.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can identify that government spending shifts AD rather than causing movement along.
questions.commonMisconception: Changes in government spending cause movement along the AD curve, not a shift.
questions.stem: The Canadian government increases infrastructure spending by $10 billion. Assuming no change in the price level initially, this will most likely cause:

options.label: A
options.text: A rightward shift of the AD curve
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Government spending is a component of AD, so an increase shifts AD rightward at every price level.

options.label: B
options.text: A leftward shift of the AD curve
options.feedbackWrong: An increase in spending shifts AD right, not left. Leftward shifts come from decreases in spending components.

options.label: C
options.text: A movement along the AD curve to a higher quantity demanded
options.feedbackWrong: Movements along AD occur only from price level changes. Government spending is a shifter, not a price.

options.label: D
options.text: No effect on AD because the price level is unchanged
options.feedbackWrong: Even if price level stays constant, the increase in G directly raises AD at all price levels, shifting the curve.

reteachModules.trigger: The student answered diagnostic question diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q1 by selecting option D: 'Household consumption (C) only'.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Aggregate demand is only household consumption spending; the other components—business investment, government spending, and net exports—are ignored.

miniLesson.explain: Aggregate demand (AD) is the total spending in the economy, composed of household consumption (C), business investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports (X - M). This matches the GDP expenditure approach. Each of the four components contributes to total demand for final goods and services. AD is not just consumption; it includes spending by all sectors of the economy.
miniLesson.example: When economists measure AD, they add up what households spend (C), what businesses invest in equipment and facilities (I), what governments purchase (G), and net exports (X - M). For instance, in our group discussion, students noted that an increase in AD raises employment and stimulates economic growth—that increase is driven by all four components together.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember 'CIG NX'—C for Consumption, I for Investment, G for Government, NX for Net exports. All four together make Aggregate Demand.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is the correct composition of aggregate demand?
guidedPractice.answer: C + I + G + (X - M) — Consumption, Investment, Government spending, and Net exports.

guidedPractice.prompt: A government builds a new highway and businesses buy new machinery. These actions directly increase which two components of aggregate demand?
guidedPractice.answer: Government spending (G) and business investment (I).

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose exports rise and imports fall. What happens to aggregate demand, and why?
guidedPractice.answer: Aggregate demand increases because net exports (X - M) rise, and net exports are a component of AD.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answers diagnostic question diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q2 incorrectly.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes the wealth effect refers only to stock market wealth or fails to understand that a higher price level reduces real wealth.

miniLesson.explain: The wealth effect is one of the three reasons the AD curve slopes downward. When the overall price level rises, the real value of money and financial assets falls, making households feel poorer and causing them to reduce consumption. This effect applies broadly to wealth, not just to stock market wealth. A lower price level increases real wealth, which boosts consumption.
miniLesson.example: When the price level rises, the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services, so households feel that their real wealth has decreased. As a result, they cut back on spending, which is why higher price levels lead to lower consumption.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Prices up → real wealth down → consumption down. The wealth effect is about purchasing power, not just stocks.

guidedPractice.prompt: According to the wealth effect, what happens to real wealth and consumption when the price level increases?
guidedPractice.answer: Real wealth falls because the purchasing power of money and assets declines, so consumption decreases.

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose the price level rises. Using the wealth effect, explain what happens to household consumption and how this relates to the downward slope of the AD curve.
guidedPractice.answer: The higher price level reduces real wealth, so households consume less. This is one of the three reasons the AD curve slopes downward: higher price levels reduce real wealth and consumption.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student says: 'The wealth effect only matters for stock market wealth, so it has little impact on aggregate demand.' Explain why this is incorrect using the three effects that make the AD curve slope downward.
guidedPractice.answer: The statement is incorrect because the wealth effect operates through the real value of all money and financial assets, not just stocks. When the price level rises, real wealth declines, reducing consumption. Together with the interest rate effect and the foreign trade effect, this explains why the AD curve slopes downward.

reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student confuses a movement along the AD curve (caused by a change in the price level) with a shift of the entire AD curve (caused by non-price factors such as government spending, money supply, or taxes).

miniLesson.explain: The AD curve is downward sloping because of the wealth effect, the interest rate effect, and the foreign trade effect. These three effects describe how a change in the price level moves the economy along the same AD curve: a lower price level increases the quantity of real GDP demanded, and a higher price level decreases it. A shift of the AD curve occurs only when there is a change in a non-price factor—that is, a change in government expenditure, the money supply, or tax rates. When one of these factors changes, the entire curve moves right or left, meaning that at every price level the total spending (C + I + G + X - M) changes.
miniLesson.example: Consider the federal government increasing infrastructure spending. This is an increase in the G component of AD, so the entire AD curve shifts right—more real GDP is demanded at every price level. In contrast, suppose the price level falls because of increased productivity. Consumers feel wealthier, interest rates fall, and net exports rise. These are movements along the same AD curve, not a shift.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Price change = slide along the curve. Policy change = shift the whole curve. Think '3 effects slide, 4 components shift when one changes.'

guidedPractice.prompt: A decrease in the price level causes a movement along the AD curve. What causes the AD curve itself to shift? Name two shifters from the lesson.
guidedPractice.answer: The AD curve shifts when there are changes in government expenditure, money supply, or tax rates. Two examples: an increase in government spending or a decrease in tax rates.

guidedPractice.prompt: If the Bank of Canada increases the money supply, does this cause a movement along the AD curve or a shift of the AD curve? Explain your reasoning.
guidedPractice.answer: An increase in the money supply shifts the AD curve to the right. The money supply is a non-price factor, not a change in the price level. At every price level, the lower interest rates from a larger money supply stimulate investment and consumption, so total spending increases.

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose Canadian consumers become more optimistic about future incomes and decide to spend more today. Is this a movement along the AD curve or a shift? Which component of AD changes, and in what direction does the curve move?
guidedPractice.answer: This is a shift of the AD curve. The increase in household consumption (C) at every price level shifts AD to the right. It is not a movement along the curve because the cause is not a change in the price level; it is a change in consumer spending behaviour.

reteachModules.trigger: Student believes that an increase in aggregate demand can permanently raise output above potential GDP in the long run.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student confuses short-run demand-driven gains with long-run supply constraints, thinking AD can permanently boost real GDP. In reality, LRAS is vertical at full-employment output, so demand changes only affect the price level in the long run.

miniLesson.explain: Aggregate demand can push output above potential in the short run, but the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve is vertical at the full-employment level of real GDP. Long-run output is determined only by supply-side factors: capital, labour, and technology. When AD rises and output exceeds potential GDP, competition for labour and raw materials drives up wages and prices, shifting SRAS upward until the economy returns to long-run equilibrium at full employment. Therefore, a permanent increase in AD does not raise real GDP in the long run—it only raises the price level.
miniLesson.example: Suppose the government increases infrastructure spending (G). In the short run, AD shifts right, firms hire more workers, and output rises above potential along the relatively flat SRAS curve. But, with output above potential, labour and raw materials become scarce, so wages and input prices are bid up. This shifts SRAS upward, and the economy moves back to the vertical LRAS at full employment. The final result is a higher price level, not a higher level of real GDP in the long run.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: LRAS is a locked door at full employment. AD can pound on it, but only 3 keys can open it: capital, labour, and technology. Without those, demand only makes prices echo.

guidedPractice.prompt: What does the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve look like, and what determines its position?
guidedPractice.answer: The LRAS curve is vertical at the full-employment level of real GDP. Its position is determined only by capital, labour, and technology, not by the price level.

guidedPractice.prompt: Suppose aggregate demand increases due to a government spending boost. Describe what happens to output and the price level in the short run and in the long run.
guidedPractice.answer: In the short run, AD shifts right, output rises above potential, and the price level rises. In the long run, because output exceeds potential, competition for labour and resources pushes wages up, shifting SRAS upward. Output returns to potential, and only the price level remains higher.

guidedPractice.prompt: Using the AD-AS model, explain why a permanent increase in aggregate demand cannot raise real GDP above potential in the long run. Include the adjustment mechanism.
guidedPractice.answer: A permanent AD increase initially raises real GDP above potential. But since LRAS is vertical at full-employment output, the economy cannot stay above potential. Excess demand for labour and raw materials bids up wages and prices, shifting SRAS upward. This adjustment continues until real GDP falls back to the vertical LRAS level. The long-run effect is a higher price level, not higher real GDP.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answered diagnostic question diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q5 incorrectly, selecting or drawing the SRAS curve as steeply upward-sloping.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve is steeply upward-sloping or even vertical, confusing it with the long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) curve. This ignores the Keynesian flat range of SRAS, where prices and wages are sticky and changes in aggregate demand primarily affect output and employment.

miniLesson.explain: In the short run, the SRAS curve is relatively flat because prices and wages are sticky. Sticky prices mean that when aggregate demand changes, firms adjust production (output and employment) rather than immediately changing prices. Therefore, an increase in AD mainly raises output and employment with only a small increase in the price level. This is different from the LRAS curve, which is vertical at full-employment output; LRAS is determined only by capital, labour, and technology, not by the price level. Drawing SRAS as a steep upward-sloping line incorrectly implies that price-level changes cause large price movements and little output response, which contradicts the Keynesian short-run behaviour.
miniLesson.example: In the Group 1 discussion, students described how an increase in AD raises employment, pushes up the price level, and stimulates economic growth. On a correctly drawn SRAS curve, the increase in AD moves along a relatively flat curve, so the main effect is higher output and employment, with only a small upward movement in the price level. If the SRAS were drawn as a steep upward-sloping line, the same increase in AD would show mostly higher prices and little output gain—which is not the short-run outcome.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of SRAS as a 'flat pancake' of sticky prices: in the short run, firms are slow to change prices, so the curve is relatively flat. In contrast, LRAS is a 'vertical wall' built on capital, labour, and technology.

guidedPractice.prompt: Fill in the blank: In the short run, the aggregate supply curve is ______ because wages and prices are ______.
guidedPractice.answer: In the short run, the SRAS curve is relatively flat because wages and prices are sticky.

guidedPractice.prompt: If the economy is in a recession and aggregate demand increases, what does the relatively flat SRAS predict about output and the price level?
guidedPractice.answer: Output (employment) increases significantly while the price level rises only slightly. The relatively flat SRAS means the extra demand is met mainly by producing more goods and services, not by raising prices, because wages and prices are sticky.

guidedPractice.prompt: Compare the SRAS curve and the LRAS curve. Why is drawing SRAS as steep upward-sloping incorrect? Use the concepts of sticky wages/prices and full-employment output in your answer.
guidedPractice.answer: SRAS is relatively flat because wages and prices are sticky, so short-run output can deviate from potential. LRAS is vertical at full-employment output and depends only on capital, labour, and technology. Drawing SRAS as steeply sloped confuses short-run price stickiness with long-run flexibility; a steep SRAS would mean price changes cause large price movements and small output changes, which ignores the Keynesian flat range and the fact that changes in AD affect output and employment in the short run.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answers diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q6 incorrectly, confusing the effects of adverse and favourable supply shocks.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes all supply shocks affect output and prices the same way, or reverses the outcomes: thinking an adverse shock increases output and a favourable shock raises unemployment.

miniLesson.explain: Supply shocks are sudden changes in production conditions that shift the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve. Adverse shocks, such as oil price spikes, reduce output, increase unemployment, and raise the price level. Favourable shocks, such as technology breakthroughs, increase output and typically do not cause inflation. In the short run, SRAS is relatively flat because wages and prices are sticky, so changes in aggregate demand or supply mainly show up in output and employment.
miniLesson.example: An oil price spike (adverse shock) shifts SRAS left: real GDP falls, unemployment rises, and the price level rises. A technology breakthrough (favourable shock) shifts SRAS right: real GDP rises, unemployment falls, and the price level stays stable or moves lower.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: A bad supply shock is a triple whammy: output down, unemployment up, prices up. A good shock does the opposite: output up, unemployment down, prices steady.

guidedPractice.prompt: Classify each event as an adverse or favourable supply shock: (a) sudden oil price spike, (b) technology breakthrough.
guidedPractice.answer: (a) Adverse, (b) Favourable.

guidedPractice.prompt: If an adverse supply shock shifts the SRAS curve left, what happens to real GDP, unemployment, and the price level?
guidedPractice.answer: Real GDP falls, unemployment rises, and the price level rises.

guidedPractice.prompt: How does a favourable supply shock affect output and prices compared to an adverse supply shock?
guidedPractice.answer: A favourable shock increases output and keeps prices stable (or lowers them), while an adverse shock reduces output and raises prices. Both shocks shift SRAS; an adverse shock shifts it left, a favourable shock shifts it right.

reteachModules.trigger: Student fails to meet rubric for question diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q7
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student cannot explain why higher output above potential leads to rising costs and a leftward shift of SRAS. They may think output can stay above potential indefinitely or that wages and prices do not adjust.

miniLesson.explain: In the short run, the SRAS curve is relatively flat because wages and prices are sticky. If aggregate demand rises enough to push output above potential GDP, the economy overheats. At output above potential, there is intense competition for labour and raw materials. This competition drives up wages and input prices, which raises production costs. Higher production costs shift the SRAS curve upward (to the left). As SRAS shifts up, the price level rises and real GDP falls back toward potential. Long-run equilibrium is restored at full employment. The LRAS curve is vertical at the full-employment level of real GDP and is determined only by capital, labour, and technology, not by the price level.
miniLesson.example: Suppose an increase in government spending shifts AD right, pushing real GDP above potential. In the short run, because wages are sticky, firms hire more workers and output rises. But with unemployment very low, firms compete for workers and bid up wages. Higher wages raise production costs, shifting SRAS upward/left. The price level rises while output falls back to potential. This adjustment can be seen in three steps: (1) output above potential, (2) rising wages and costs, (3) SRAS shifts up until output returns to potential.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember the 4-step wage spiral: Overheating → Wage competition → Costs rise → SRAS shifts up and output falls back. Think of a too-tight balloon: if you blow too much (above potential), pressure (wages) builds until the balloon resists and returns to its natural size.

guidedPractice.prompt: When the economy is producing above potential GDP, what happens in the market for labour and raw materials?
guidedPractice.answer: Competition for labour and raw materials drives up wages and prices, increasing production costs.

guidedPractice.prompt: An increase in aggregate demand pushes real GDP above potential. In the short run, wages eventually rise. What happens to the SRAS curve, the price level, and real GDP?
guidedPractice.answer: Higher wages and input costs shift the SRAS curve upward (to the left). The price level rises, and real GDP falls back toward potential GDP.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain the complete short-run to long-run adjustment mechanism after a positive AD shock, including the roles of wages, SRAS, and real GDP.
guidedPractice.answer: A positive AD shock raises output above potential in the short run. Because unemployment is low, firms compete for workers, pushing wages up. Higher wages and raw material costs increase production costs, shifting SRAS upward/left. As SRAS shifts, the price level rises while real GDP returns to potential, restoring long-run equilibrium at full employment.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists ALL four components that make up aggregate demand in an economy?
options: Consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports
Consumption and investment only
Consumption, savings, government spending, and exports
Consumption, investment, government spending, and imports

questions.stem: In a country, households spend $500 billion, businesses invest $200 billion, government spends $300 billion, exports are $150 billion, and imports are $100 billion. Calculate the economy's aggregate demand. Then explain why it would be incorrect to say that aggregate demand equals household consumption alone.
questions.rubric: Correct calculation: AD = C + I + G + (X - M) = 500 + 200 + 300 + (150 - 100) = $1050 billion. Explanation must state that aggregate demand includes not only consumption but also investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports (X - M). Household consumption alone ($500 billion) omits the other components and would significantly understate total spending.

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer Question 1 correctly (select option A) and provide a correct calculation plus clear explanation in Question 2, mentioning all four components and why consumption alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: Inflation causes the price level to rise significantly. As a result, the real value of money held in savings accounts and cash falls. Based on the wealth effect, how would households most likely respond?
options: They will increase spending because they feel wealthier from having more money.
They will decrease spending because their real wealth has fallen.
They will spend the same amount because the wealth effect only applies to stocks.
They will borrow more to maintain their real wealth.

questions.stem: Explain how the wealth effect contributes to the downward slope of the aggregate demand curve. Define 'real wealth' in your answer and use an example that does not involve the stock market.
questions.rubric: Full credit (3/3): Response correctly defines real wealth as the purchasing power of money and assets. Explains that a higher price level reduces real wealth, causing consumption to fall, and links this to a lower quantity of real GDP demanded (moving along the AD curve). Provides a clear non-stock example (e.g., cash, savings accounts, bonds). Partial credit (2/3): Correctly identifies the causal chain but example is stock market or unclear. Partial credit (1/3): Mentions wealth effect but confuses direction or misses key link. No credit (0): Repeats misconception that wealth effect only applies to stocks or that price level increases wealth.

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer Question 1 correctly (select option B) and earn at least 2/3 on Question 2 rubric.

questions.stem: Which of the following events causes a shift of the aggregate demand (AD) curve rather than a movement along it?
options: A decrease in the price level increases the real value of money and boosts consumption.
The government increases spending on infrastructure, raising total spending at every price level.
A lower domestic price level makes exports cheaper, increasing net exports.
Higher price levels increase the demand for money, raising interest rates and reducing investment.

questions.stem: Explain why a fall in the price level leads to a movement along the AD curve, while an increase in government spending leads to a shift of the entire AD curve. In your answer, identify the specific aggregate demand components affected and the direction of any curve shift.
questions.rubric: The response must correctly distinguish a movement along the AD curve (caused solely by a change in the price level, operating through the wealth, interest rate, or foreign trade effects) from a shift of the AD curve (caused by non-price factors such as government spending, money supply, or taxes). It should state that a fall in the price level moves the economy down the existing AD curve, while an increase in government spending (a component of G) shifts the AD curve to the right. The response should reference at least two of the three price-level effects and identify that the shift is rightward.

retestCards.passRule: The student must select option B in Question 1 and provide a response to Question 2 that correctly explains the difference between a movement along and a shift of the AD curve, including at least one price-level effect (wealth, interest rate, or foreign trade) and the direction of the shift for an increase in government spending (rightward).

questions.stem: Assume an economy is currently producing at its full-employment level. If business confidence improves permanently and firms increase investment (I), which outcome best describes the long-run equilibrium?
options: Real GDP remains at potential GDP, and the price level is permanently higher.
Real GDP rises above potential GDP and stays there because AD has shifted right.
Real GDP returns to potential GDP, and the price level returns to its original level.
Real GDP falls below potential GDP, and the price level falls.

questions.stem: Explain why a permanent increase in aggregate demand cannot increase real GDP above potential output in the long run. Use the concepts of long-run aggregate supply (LRAS), short-run aggregate supply (SRAS), and the adjustment that occurs when output is above full employment.
questions.rubric: 4 points: (1) States LRAS is vertical at full-employment GDP and determined by supply-side factors (capital, labour, technology); (2) Explains a permanent AD increase initially raises output above potential and raises the price level; (3) Explains above-potential output drives up wages and resource prices, shifting SRAS upward/leftward; (4) Concludes real GDP returns to potential GDP, leaving only the price level permanently higher. Score 3 or 4 passes.

retestCards.passRule: Q1 must be answered correctly, and Q2 must score at least 3 out of 4 on the rubric.

questions.stem: Which diagram best represents the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve according to the Keynesian view?
options: A vertical line at full-employment output
A relatively flat line because wages and prices are sticky
A steep upward-sloping line because wages adjust quickly
A downward-sloping line because lower prices increase real wealth

questions.stem: Using the concepts of sticky wages/prices and the distinction between SRAS and LRAS, explain why drawing the SRAS curve as steeply upward-sloping is inaccurate.
questions.rubric: Accept answers that include at least two of the following key ideas: (1) SRAS is relatively flat in the short run; (2) wages and prices are sticky, meaning firms adjust output/employment before changing prices; (3) a steep SRAS would imply large price changes and small output changes, which is not the short-run result; (4) LRAS is vertical at full-employment output and depends on capital, labour, and technology, not the price level.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct answer in Q1 and in Q2 explain that SRAS is relatively flat because wages and prices are sticky, and that a steep SRAS confuses short-run behaviour with the long-run vertical LRAS. Accept if at least two of the rubric's key ideas are present.

questions.stem: A severe drought destroys crops across a country. Which macroeconomic outcome is most likely?
options: Favourable supply shock: real GDP rises and the price level falls
Adverse supply shock: real GDP falls and the price level rises
Adverse demand shock: real GDP and the price level both fall
Favourable demand shock: real GDP and the price level both rise

questions.stem: A breakthrough in renewable energy technology sharply lowers production costs for many industries. Explain how this favourable supply shock affects real GDP, employment, and the price level in the short run, and describe the shift in the SRAS curve.
questions.rubric: Student must state that the favourable supply shock shifts SRAS to the right; real GDP increases, unemployment decreases (or employment rises), and the price level stays stable or decreases. If they describe only some of these elements, award partial credit.

retestCards.passRule: Q1 must be answered correctly (option B). Q2 must correctly identify the SRAS shift and at least two of the three effects: real GDP up, employment up, price level stable/down.

questions.stem: An economy is booming, and real GDP is currently above potential GDP. Which long-run adjustment is most consistent with the AD-AS model?
options: Wages and input prices rise, shifting SRAS upward/left, and real GDP falls back to potential.
The LRAS curve shifts right, permanently locking in the higher output.
Real GDP stays above potential because firms can always expand production.
Aggregate demand automatically falls, and no cost adjustments occur.

questions.stem: Suppose the government increases spending, shifting AD to the right and pushing real GDP above full-employment output. Use the AD-AS model to explain the step-by-step adjustment that returns the economy to long-run equilibrium. In your answer, include what happens to wages, the SRAS curve, the price level, and real GDP.
questions.rubric: Award 1 point for each of the following, up to 5: (1) Output above potential creates competition for labour and raw materials; (2) Wages and input prices rise; (3) SRAS shifts upward/to the left; (4) Price level rises; (5) Real GDP decreases back to potential GDP. A complete answer must show the causal chain, not just list terms. Minimum 4/5 to pass.

retestCards.passRule: Q1 must be correct (option A). Q2 must score at least 4/5 on the rubric. Both required to pass.

dashboardFormat.objective: Aggregate demand (AD) is the total spending in the economy, composed of household consumption (C), business investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports (X - M), matching the GDP expenditure approach.；The AD curve slopes downward due to three effects: the wealth effect (higher price levels reduce real wealth and consumption), the interest rate effect (higher prices increase demand for money, raising interest rates and reducing investment), and the foreign trade effect (higher domestic prices reduce net exports).；The AD curve shifts when there are changes in government expenditure, money supply, or tax rates (factors beyond the price level).

learningGoals.statement: Identify and explain the components of aggregate demand and the reasons for the downward-sloping AD curve.
Distinguish between movements along the AD curve and shifts of the AD curve.
Explain the difference between short-run and long-run aggregate supply and the transition to long-run equilibrium.
Analyze the effects of supply shocks on output, employment, and the price level.

nextActions: [err-AD-onlyC] Student answers question diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q1 incorrectly: You identified aggregate demand as only consumption. Remember, AD is the total spending and includes business investment, government purchases, and net exports too.

[err-AD-wealth-misconception] Student answers question diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q2 incorrectly: The wealth effect operates through changes in the real value of money and financial assets, not just stock market wealth.

[err-AD-slope-vs-shift] Student answers question diag-cia4u-s6-0803-q3 incorrectly: Changes in government spending shift the AD curve; they do not cause movement along it. Price level changes cause movements.

cards.question: Aggregate demand (AD) is composed of which of the following sets of spending components?
options: Household consumption (C), business investment (I), government spending (G), net exports (X - M)
Business investment (I) and government spending (G) only
Household consumption (C) and government spending (G) only
Household consumption (C) only
Business investment (I) and net exports (X - M) only
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows AD includes investment, government, and net exports beyond consumption.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! AD equals C + I + G + (X - M), matching the expenditure approach to GDP.
This omits consumption and net exports. AD includes all spending on final goods and services.
Investment and net exports are also part of AD. Think of the expenditure formula for GDP.
Consumption is the largest component, but AD includes business investment, government spending, and net exports as well.
Consumption and government spending are also part of AD. AD is the total of all spending sectors.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies all four components of aggregate demand (C+I+G+NX).
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.
cards.alignmentNote: AD components are part of macroeconomic models in D1.
cards.commonMisconception: Aggregate demand only refers to household consumption spending.

cards.question: According to the wealth effect, a decrease in the overall price level will:
options: Increase the real value of money and financial assets, leading to more consumption
Decrease the purchasing power of money, reducing consumption
Only affect stock market wealth but not real spending
Have no effect on consumption because wages are sticky
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of the wealth effect mechanism.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! A lower price level increases real wealth, encouraging households to spend more.
A decrease in the price level actually increases purchasing power. The wealth effect works in the opposite direction.
The wealth effect applies to the real value of all nominal assets, not just stocks. It affects overall consumption.
Sticky wages affect supply, not the wealth effect. The wealth effect operates through real balances and assets.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies the wealth effect as operating through real wealth changes due to price level changes.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of various macroeconomic models and measures, including indicators used to measure economic inequalities, and assess their usefulness.
cards.alignmentNote: Wealth effect is part of the downward-sloping AD curve in macroeconomic models.
cards.commonMisconception: The wealth effect refers only to financial asset values or stock market wealth.

cards.question: The Canadian government increases infrastructure spending by $10 billion. Assuming no change in the price level initially, this will most likely cause:
options: A rightward shift of the AD curve
A leftward shift of the AD curve
A movement along the AD curve to a higher quantity demanded
No effect on AD because the price level is unchanged
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can identify that government spending shifts AD rather than causing movement along.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! Government spending is a component of AD, so an increase shifts AD rightward at every price level.
An increase in spending shifts AD right, not left. Leftward shifts come from decreases in spending components.
Movements along AD occur only from price level changes. Government spending is a shifter, not a price.
Even if price level stays constant, the increase in G directly raises AD at all price levels, shifting the curve.
cards.successCriteria: Student distinguishes a shift of AD from a movement along AD caused by price level change.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of fiscal policy in Canada, including how it is shaped and its impact.
cards.alignmentNote: AD shifters like government spending are fiscal policy tools from D2.
cards.commonMisconception: Changes in government spending cause movement along the AD curve, not a shift.
